Q: Visual Studio 2026 Insider Preview Javascript Errors A:

For me, in newer VS 2026 version (18.3.0, Insiders [11426.168]), checking option Javascript/TypeScript -> Language Service -> General -> Disable dedicated syntax process (restart required) and restarting Visual Studio did the trick. Note: the option is located in legacy options menu.

Q: How does DP provide optimization over backtracking in 0-1 Knapsack problem A:

Draw a 2-dimensional table with one dimension for the sack capacity and one dimension for the items.

Then draw your recursion tree diagram on that grid and see how it overlaps with that grid: many of the branches of the tree end up in superposition, which means redundant calculations.

These calculations are only made once with DP, so you end up with

complexity = (number of items) * (weight precision)

with DP, instead of

complexity = 2^(number of items)

with simple recursion.

Q: Unable to torch.load due to pickling/safety error A:

I see two main issues here:

  1. The checkpoint that you are trying to load contains instances of NumPy 1.x classes/functions, while you are trying to load it in an environment with NumPy 2.x.
  2. The checkpoint that you are trying to load contains an actual model rather than model weights only.

As to 1

A lot of changes, some of them breaking changes, happened in the step from NumPy 1.x to NumPy 2.x, one of them being privatizing the numpy.core namespace. That is, classes that could be found under numpy.core in NumPy 1.x are now under numpy._core. Luckily, add_safe_globals() and safe_globals() provide a mechanism to handle this situation (emphasis by me):

Each item in the list can either be a function/class or a tuple of the form (function/class, string) where string is the full path of the function/class.

Here, function/class refers to the new location and name (_core in the given case), while string refers to the old location and name (core in the given case) of the function/class of interest.

As to 2

It seems like someone stored a complete model instance as part of their checkpoint (torch.save({"model": model, …}) rather than the model weights only (torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), …}). As a consequence, rather than only loading PyTorch tensors and scalars, which are considered safe by default, we have to allow all components that are used in the model itself (e.g. torch.nn.modules.batchnorm.BatchNorm2d or models.yolo.Model) via add_safe_globals()/ safe_globals().

Putting it all together

I was able to load the model of the given checkpoint with the following code:

import os, numpy as np, torch
from yolov5 import models

checkpoint_path = os.path.expanduser("~/Downloads/signatureyolo.pt")  # TODO: Adjust

with torch.serialization.safe_globals([
        (np._core.multiarray._reconstruct, "numpy.core.multiarray._reconstruct"),
        np.ndarray,
        np.dtype,
        np.dtypes.Float64DType,
        torch.nn.modules.container.Sequential,
        torch.nn.modules.container.ModuleList,
        torch.nn.modules.conv.Conv2d,
        torch.nn.modules.batchnorm.BatchNorm2d,
        torch.nn.modules.activation.SiLU,
        torch.nn.modules.pooling.MaxPool2d,
        torch.nn.modules.upsampling.Upsample,
        (models.yolo.DetectionModel, "models.yolo.Model"),
        (models.yolo.Detect, "models.yolo.Detect"),
        (models.common.Focus, "models.common.Focus"),
        (models.common.Conv, "models.common.Conv"),
        (models.common.C3, "models.common.C3"),
        (models.common.Bottleneck, "models.common.Bottleneck"),
        (models.common.SPP, "models.common.SPP"),
        (models.common.Concat, "models.common.Concat"),
    ]):
    ckpt = torch.load(checkpoint_path, weights_only=True, map_location="cpu")

print(ckpt)
# {'epoch': -1, 'best_fitness': array([    0.49472]), 'training_results': None, 'model': DetectionModel(
#   (model): Sequential(
#     (0): Focus(
#       (conv): Conv(
#         (conv): Conv2d(12, 80, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1), bias=False)
#         (bn): BatchNorm2d(80, eps=0.001, momentum=0.03, affine=True, track_running_stats=True)
#         (act): SiLU()
# ...

My environment (essential parts):

  • Python 3.13.9
  • PyTorch 2.10.0
  • NumPy 2.4.1
  • YOLOv5 7.0.14

To get rid of the hassle, I would suggest saving your own version of the checkpoint, ensuring that only native Python classes and PyTorch tensors are contained (and, in particular, using model.state_dict() rather than model – see above).

Q: How to execute bitwise operators in Brainfuck? A:

I wrote the winning answer for the question you got referred to in a comment. You'll notice that that one wants roughly 30 free space to the right. A similar approach could work with more like 18 or 20 space, but 5 space (or 7 in total) is really cramped for this kind of thing. That'll force you to extract only one bit at a time, and it probably makes your code longer and maybe also slower. (Note that all the people who generated brainfuck from another language so far have produced really bloated code.)

As a start point for what you want to do, though, have a look at this code I wrote for asm2bf.

1[l+1-]2[1+n+2-]1[2+1-]e+l[>>[-[->>+<]<]<[>>>+<<]<[-[->>+<]<]>>[>-<<]>>[+[--<<<e[d+1+e-]o]]p[l+p-]e[<+>-]<[>++<-]>l]n[-]e[-] (AND)

1[l+1-]2[1+n+2-]1[2+1-]e+l[>>[-[->>+<]<]<[>>>+<<]<[-[->>+<]<]>>[>-<<]>>+[<<<e[d+1+e-]o[-]]p[l+p-]e[<+>-]<[>++<-]>l]n[e[d+1+e-]d[>+<-]n-]e[-] (OR)

1[l+1-]2[1+n+2-]1[2+1-]e+l[>>[-[->>+<]<]<[>>>-<<]<[-[->>+<]<]>>[>-<<]>>+[<<<e[d+1+e-]o+[-]]p[l+p-]e[<+>-]<[>++<-]>l]n[e[d+1+e-]d[>+<-]n-]e[-] (XOR)

In this, letters and numbers mean to move the pointer to that cell; cells "1" and "2" hold the operands initially, cells "d" and "e" are consecutive, and cells "k", "l", "m", "n", "o", "p" are consecutive. So that's ten cells used; this one replaces operand "1" with the result.

Obvious ways to save cells are: use a bit-extraction algorithm that only wants one navigational zero and not two; reuse a zero from that chunk in place of cell "d"; don't save operand "2" (maybe reuse that space for "e" or something). This could get you down to seven. But you see what I mean about the lack of space.
